page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard3.Flex.16-64 is a compute instance belonging to the Standard family. It is powered by an Intel Xeon 8358 processor operating at a base clock speed of 2.6 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The server provides 16 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading, totaling 32 dedicated vCPUs. System memory is provisioned at 64.0 GB, resulting in a memory-to-vCPU density of 2.0 GB per thread.

The architecture is designed around dedicated CPU allocation rather than shared or burstable cores. The instance does not bundle local NVMe or SSD storage, necessitating the use of remote block storage services for persistent file systems and databases. No discrete GPU hardware is present. Network provisioning includes one complimentary public IPv4 address for direct ingress and egress routing.

Given its 1:2 memory-to-vCPU ratio and high core density, this profile represents a compute-focused configuration. Cost efficiency is driven by high execution throughput across 32 threads without allocating unused memory capacity. It is primarily suited for compute-intensive workloads such as distributed continuous integration pipelines, software build compilation, video transcoding, and batch data processing.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard3.Flex.16-64 is an x86_64 compute-oriented virtual machine featuring an Intel Xeon 8358 processor clocked at 2.6 GHz. The configuration provides 16 physical cores and 32 dedicated vCPUs via two threads per core, alongside 64.0 GB of system memory. This yields a 1:2 memory-to-vCPU allocation of 2.0 GB per thread. The server does not bundle local disk storage or GPU accelerators, relying on network-attached storage for stateful operations. A single complimentary public IPv4 address is included for networking. With dedicated compute cores and a lean memory envelope, VM.Standard3.Flex.16-64 is well aligned with compute-bound workloads, including distributed build jobs, parallel batch computation, CI/CD runners, and web application worker tiers.
